doc.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

title: Peace message, Lonnie Liston Smith, and finding Jon Lucien at the Blue Note
summary: He calls musicians soldiers for peace, meets Lonnie Liston Smith, then tells how he searched for Jon Lucien in New York and eventually reached the Blue Note green room, introducing himself as his son.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: and you come to a concert or something and you hear something that’s really beautiful and in your deepest and darkest moment you remember that experience that caused you such elation at that point in time. Take a piece of it with you. Take it with you you know. Let it manifest, let it change your life. We are not here — we are the soldiers for peace and harmony and for a better world. When, I always remember, you know that poem if the rest of the world is losing their head and you can keep your head about you then yours is the world my son. And if, as we see in our environment today the way global leaders are treating people and speaking about their desire to not recognize the plight of others, I mean you know we are the ones that have to send that message out strongly because this is who we are. We are global citizens. Music doesn’t belong to any one person you know. It’s there for all. And there’s no other language that brings people together like music. There’s nothing. You know I’ve lived it myself that you know, where music has touched my soul or a performer has touched my soul and brought about this immense change in me, like Don Alias and Emile Latimer. I mean I will leave the planet with that in my heart, hoping that I will be able to see them in the next realm when I get there. Because I know Emile is waiting for me. I know — I did his memorial. I lived one of my greatest musical dreams being the percussionist for Jon Lucien. I mean Jon was one of the few guys from the Caribbean to like take the jazz world and in the late 70s into the 80s etcetera, I mean his music, Jon’s music brought me through college, brought me through university, through my darkest time. Him, Lonnie Liston Smith, you know, and I just met Lonnie. I drove — I hadn’t seen or heard from Lonnie in over thirty years. And I drove, I was looking up something and I came across Keystone Corner in Baltimore and I saw Lonnie Liston Smith. And I left the house, I jumped in the car and I drove four hours to Baltimore to see and meet one of the guys who I revered for his cosmic — he was my cosmic jazz master. You know? And listen, when he hugged me, you know I’m 62 now I mean to get a hug from one of your icons, and I was like — I don’t know if you listen to music but I want you to know how much you influenced me etcetera etcetera. And I brought a CD of mine just so that you can hear. And I’m reaching into my jacket pocket to try and pull out the CD and I’m so nervous and I’m going to see him perform and I’m standing there with one of my cards, and he’s helping me to pull the CD out of my shirt. And oh listen, and Jon Lucien was another guy like that man. Jon took me through university. I mean I listened to that guy [scats]. I mean listen, I fed off of that music and it was — I had — when I came to New York I searched for Jon left, right and center. He was nowhere to be found. He had stopped performing. He was in rehab. He was all over the world etcetera until a friend of mine many many years later said, “Hey Cascadu, I saw,” because everybody knew that I was a Jon Lucien fanatic, right? “Hey Cascadu, I just saw a poster at LIU for Jon Lucien.” I said, “What!” Okay it means he’s got to be in © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-

town. If you saw it, right, because it had passed already. He’s got to be in town. And I looked up and I saw he was at the Blue Note. I hauled my butt down to the Blue Note that night man, and I went to the Blue Note, and I got there early, super early. I was one of the first people getting into the Blue Note. And Jon came onto the stage, this frail guy man. This frail guy. And I’m looking at him and I’m like this is the man, this is the moment I waited for and that band kicked off [scats] and his pipes came out, that soft, velvety, deep baritone man. And I was in seventh heaven. At the end of the show — I stayed for the second show and at the end of the show I was like, what do I do? I can’t leave. I’ve got to connect with this guy. I’ve waited all these years, so many years have passed, over thirty years, to meet this guy. I’d never seen him. And I was scared. I didn’t know what to do, how do I get up to the room to say hello? So I had a decision — you leave and you walk away from this just having seen your idol, or you go upstairs and you connect with him. And I got up — I walked up the stairs at the Blue Note man, and I got to the green room and the door was closed but I could hear all the musicians, there’s all laughter and chatter and everything else going on. And I knocked on the door. And I heard, “Who go there?” And the door swings open. One of the musicians had — ‘cause they’re all sitting down in rows like this, right. So somebody opened the door this way and Jon is sitting in one of those big Indonesian rattan chairs, sitting like a king in the chair, all these musicians on the side here, and there’s a pathway, a very narrow pathway leading straight to the door. I am at the door and Jon is sitting straight in front of me. And I said, when, you know, “Who go there” and the door opens, I said, “Mr. Lucien, I am your son!” I didn’t know what else to say, because this man had fathered my music, he had fathered my heart, he had fathered my creativity. I listened to all his musicians, I played his records day in, day out man, anywhere I went I spoke about Jon Lucien, spoke about the beauty of his music, I mean this guy was like my life. You know? And all of a sudden, I didn’t know what to say. I was scared. And I said, “Mr. Lucien my name is Cascadu. I’m your son.” And Jon got up from the chair. He got up and there was a woman sitting right next to him who I later found out was his wife. He got up from the chair. The musicians in the room went dead silent. You could hear a rat piss on cotton in the far corner of the hall. Everybody was dead silent. Silence in the room. Jon got up. He looked at his wife like this, and he said, “Come my son.” And I walked into Jon’s arms. I was shaking. I walked into my idol’s arms and he did not let me go. He held onto me like you would not believe man. And I just grabbed onto him. And there were no words coming out of my mouth at that point in time. The room was silent. All his big musicians were standing, sitting right there. His wife sitting right there. And we just, in this embrace, locked in this embrace. And there was nothing to tell me that this was anything other than one of the most divine moments of my life. I could feel like there was energy just coming down and bathing us © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
